title: The Babylonian Expedition of the University of Pennsylvania Vol. 2

p: PROFESSOR HENRY EYSTER JACOBS, D.D., LL.D.
This volume contains one hundred and fifteen plates of autograph texts and eight plates of Aramaic endorsements.

This volume of texts, from the Murashu archives, completes those dated in the reign of Darius II, with the exception of a number which are in private possession. The number of the unpublished documents is about two-thirds as many as contained in this volume, and are dated in the reign of Artaxerxes I. With the exception of the Aramaic endorsements scratched or written on the documents which are too poorly preserved to be reproduced, all that are found on the tablets of the archives in the University Museum and the Constantinople Museum, including those not reproduced in Vol. IX B. E., are brought together, and are found on eight plates following the texts of this volume. The translations of the endorsements, which are not discussed in the Harper Memorial Volumes, where most of them were published, are found in the "Description of Aramaic Endorsements." In the previous volume I was able to identify a large number of Persian names by the help of Justi Iranisches Namenbuch, but not being an Iranian scholar, I preferred to seek the help of Prof. C. C. Torrey and Dr. Louis H. Gray in making the identifications for this volume. In connection with each name identified or discussed by them I have added their names. I take this occasion to thank them for their kind assistance. The identifications of the Persian names previously made, are not repeated in this volume. Several Egyptian names have also been identified by Prof. Hermann Ranke of Heidelberg. His results are published in his valuable monograph Keilschriftliches Material zur Altagyptischen Vokalisation, in the Proceedings of the Royal Prussian Academy. It was my purpose to give the translations of selected texts which differ from those of. the two previous volumes, but preferring to give all the remaining texts of Darius' reign, I have postponed publishing the translations, especially because of the size of the volume.

About fifty of the texts of this volume were copied in Constantinople from tablets which have been retained in the Ottoman Museum. They were copied during the month of June, 1909. In this connection I desire to* express my thanks for the courtesies extended me while at work in the Museum by their Excellencies, the late Dr. O. Hamdy Bey, and his brother Halil Bey, as well as the General Secretary of the Museum, Nicolaki Efendi Ohanny. I desire also to thank the Director of the University Museum, Prof. George B. Gordon, Sc.D., for his encouragement and assistance in the pursuit of my labors. ALBERT T. CLAY. University of Pennsylvania, May 10, 1910.

The administrative documents of these archives, like the letters, are generally written in a legible hand. In copying the tablets the roughness of the surface, due to the moisture in the ground, or exposure to the atmosphere after being excavated, has not been reproduced when the writing was perfectly clear. This method of copying seems preferable, for otherwise the reading of the texts is often rendered more difficult than the reading of the originals. As was said in the previous volumes no effort has been made to determine the reigns of the undated or fragmentary tablets. When it is possible to date them the reign can easily be ascertained by noting in what dated documents, of those published in Vol. XIV B. E., and this volume, the names on the tablets in question occur. Naturally, in most cases the dates can only be fixed approximately, because the names of individuals are in many cases found on tablets dated in more than one reign. Several additional minor gains for the understanding of the chronology of the Cassite period result from a study of the documents of these archives. Tablet No. 134 is dated on the 22d day of Shebet in the 2yth year of a reign not mentioned. The question arises to which reign does this document belong and especially as the highest dated tablet of the previous volume was written in the 25th year. Unfortunately it contains only two names which can be used in dating the tablet. Ilu-iddina occurs on text 132, which must have been written between the middle of the reign of Nazi-Maruttash and Shagarakti-Shuriash. It occurs also on Vol. XIV B. E., 13:3, which was written in the 5th year of Kuri-Galzu. The other name Tu-ra-ilu occurs on Vol. XIV B. E., 24:11, which was written in the i6th year of Kuri-Galzu. It would seem, therefore, that the tablet in question, namely No. 134, probably belongs either to the reign of Kuri-Galzu, or to Nazi-Maruttash, who ruled according to the King's list, 2 5. and 26 years respectively.

UNIV. MTTS. BABYL. SEC. Another tablet, C. B. S. 11109, is dated on the 4th day of Nisan in the 2yth year. The name of Enlil-kidinni is mentioned on this tablet. This individual appears in the documents of the reign of BurnaBuriash. It is, therefore, safe to say that the reign of this monarch extended into the 27th year, which had already been assumed by others, but on the basis of the previous tablet, which, as we have seen above, belongs to a succeeding reign. Another tablet, No. 43, records the payment of aklum for the days between the 2ist of Sivan and the 25th of Tammuz of the yth year of Kadashman-Enlil. This is the year following the latest dated tablet of this reign in the previous volume. C. B. S. 13516 is dated still later in the same year, namely, the 2ist day of the 8th month. With one notable exception the tablets of this volume do not contain important impressions of seals. This one contains an unusually large seal, one of the oldest representations of the plow known.

It is found on text No. 20, which is dated in the 4th year of NaziMaruttash (i4th century B. C.), the seal having been run over both sides of the tablet as well as the four edges. Unfortunately there is no complete impression of the seal on the tablet. Some parts were repeated several times, but others are wanting. Moreover, owing to the moisture in the earth and exposure to the atmosphere since it was excavated, the surface of the tablet has suffered considerably. A yoke of oxen is represented drawing the plow. The name of the animal is alpu"ox" in the inscriptions and is called at the present time, zebu, or humped bull (bos indicus). 1 Three men are employed in operating the plow; one guides it; another drives the animals, who being depicted larger in size than the others is doubtless the chief of the gang; and a third, with a bag of grain on his shoulder, is in the
